output.title: Before-and-after framing hides the middle
output.body:
The quiet cost of before-and-after framing is that it makes a workflow look cleaner than it is. A small business owner sees “before manual invoicing, after automation” and is asked to trust a finish line without looking at the middle. That middle is where the real work lives: setup, learning, integration friction, and the handoff from a demo to daily use. A slide can skip it. A workflow cannot.

For a bounded Bareni decision, I would start with one recurring workflow and ask whether it is repeatable enough to test. That is what the free 30-minute diagnostic is for: identify the one recurring workflow, say honestly whether AI fits, and, if it does, define pilot scope, fixed price, and measures. The point is not to promise an outcome. It is to separate a paper before-and-after from a working one.

A practical next step is simple: write down one process you repeat every week and note what would count as success before you commit. If you cannot name that in plain English, the “after” is still just a story.

The real before-and-after test happens inside your workflow, not in a vendor demo.
